language_wrapper:
On an {size}×{size} board, a black or a white stone is placed on each square. A move consists of choosing one row and one column and reversing the color of every stone in the union of that row and column (the intersection stone is reversed exactly once). Determine the largest integer N such that, regardless of the initial arrangement of stones, it is always possible to perform a sequence of such moves so that the number of black stones on the board is at least N. After solving the above problem, please output your final answer in the following format:
### The final answer is: $\boxed{<your answer>}$
hardness_rationale: The seed problem fixes a 19×19 board. This family elevates the difficulty by requiring a proof for an arbitrary odd n×n board. The solution uses a nontrivial linear-algebraic identity (a four-corners move decomposition) to constructively blacken an (n−1)×(n−1) interior without disturbing previously fixed cells, and a global parity invariant on specially chosen row–column unions to show optimality. Handling arbitrary n forces contestants to generalize invariants, control border effects, and reason about parity constraints systematically, which is significantly more sophisticated than solving a single-size instance.
notes:
Proof of correctness (for odd n):
- Definitions. Represent colors as 0/1 in GF(2). A move at (i,j) toggles exactly the union of row i and column j, with the intersection (i,j) toggled once; denote this operation by O_{i,j}.

- Key identity (four corners). For any i < n and j < n, the combination O_{i,j} + O_{i,n} + O_{n,j} + O_{n,n} toggles exactly the four corner cells (i,j), (i,n), (n,j), (n,n). In particular, among interior cells, only (i,j) is affected. This identity allows us to toggle a specific interior cell while confining collateral changes to the last row/last column and the bottom-right corner.

- Lower bound construction. Start with any arrangement. For each white cell (i,j) in the (n−1)×(n−1) interior (1 ≤ i,j ≤ n−1), apply the four-corners combination above to flip (i,j) to black. These operations do not alter any other interior cell. After processing all interior whites, the interior is entirely black. The remaining cells lie in the union of the last row and the last column, which contains 2n−1 cells. Among any set of cells, a single move O_{n,n} complements all colors in this union, so by possibly applying O_{n,n}, we can ensure at least ceil((2n−1)/2) = n black stones within this union. Therefore, we can enforce at least (n−1)^2 + n = n^2 − n + 1 black stones in total.

- Upper bound via parity invariants. Consider the adversarial initial configuration: the last row is entirely black and all other cells are white. Fix any 1 ≤ i ≤ n−1 and 1 ≤ j ≤ n−1, and let S(i,j) be the set consisting of the union of row i and column j, excluding the intersection (i,j). Observe that any move toggles an even number of stones within S(i,j):
  * If the chosen move is neither row i nor column j, exactly two stones of S(i,j) are toggled (one in row i and one in column j), preserving parity.
  * If the move targets the intersection (i,j), it toggles exactly |S(i,j)| = 2n−2 stones of S(i,j), parity preserved.
  * If the move targets row i but not column j (or vice versa), it toggles n−1 stones of S(i,j), but since n is odd, n−1 is even; parity preserved.
Thus, the parity of the number of white stones in S(i,j) is invariant under all moves. Initially, S(i,j) consists of all whites in row i and column j except (i,j); since the unique black in this union is (n,j), S(i,j) has exactly 2n−3 white stones, which is odd when n is odd. Therefore, at every stage, S(i,j) must contain at least one white stone.

Suppose we could exceed n^2 − n + 1 black stones. Then at most n−2 whites remain. By pigeonhole, there are at least two rows and at least two columns containing no whites. Choose any i ≤ n−1 and any j ≤ n−1 among such rows and columns. Then S(i,j) would have zero whites, contradicting the invariant that S(i,j) must contain an odd (thus nonzero) number of whites. Hence, no sequence of moves can guarantee more than n^2 − n + 1 black stones for this adversarial start.

- Conclusion. The constructive lower bound and the invariant-based upper bound match, yielding the exact largest guaranteed number N = n^2 − n + 1 for odd n.

Implementation notes:
- The generator enforces odd n (≥ 9) to ensure invariants (e.g., parity of n−1) are even and the proof applies cleanly.
- The verifier recomputes the closed-form answer n^2 − n + 1 and returns it in the requested boxed format.
source_question:
On a 19*19 board, a black or a white stone is placed on each of the 361 squares. An operation consists of choosing one row and one column and reversing the color of all 37 stones in that row and column. Find the largest integer n such that, regardless of the initial arrangement of stones, it is always possible to perform a sequence of such operations so that the number of black stones on the board is at least n.
After solving the above problem, please output your final answer in the following format:
### The final answer is: $\boxed{<your answer>}$
Example:
### The final answer is: $\boxed{123}$
The final answer should be given as precisely as possible (using LaTeX symbols such as \sqrt, \frac, \pi, etc.). If the final answer involves a decimal approximation, it must be accurate to at least four decimal places.
source_answer: First, consider the $18\times18$ space in the upper-left corner. Select a point and perform one operation on all 35 pieces of its row and column, then this point is affected by 35 operations, its color flipped; other points in the same row or column with it are operated on 18 times, and points not in the same row and column with it are operated on 2 times, their colors unchanged. Therefore, for each white piece in the upper-left $18\times18$, one can operate in this way, such that all pieces on the cells of the upper-left $18\times18$ become black. Consider the remaining 37 cells. If after the transformation of making all pieces on the cells in the upper-left $18\times18$ black, the number of black pieces among them is less than or equal to 18, then perform one operation on the bottom-rightmost cell, and the number of black pieces will be greater than or equal to 19. Therefore, whatever the initial placement, it is possible through some number of operations to make the number of black pieces be greater than or equal to $18\times18+19=343$. Assume any initial placement can be operated on to make the number of black pieces reach 344. Consider such an initial placement: initially, the last row is black pieces, and the rest are all white pieces. If after the operations the number of black pieces is greater than or equal to 344, then the number of white pieces is less than or equal to 17, and therefore there exist two rows and two columns with no white pieces. Select a row that is not the last row and a column, and consider all the cells of this row and column besides the intersection point: these cells have no white pieces after the transformation, whereas before the transformation they had exactly 1 black piece. However, we can prove that for the set composed of these 36 cells of this row and column, besides the intersection point, the parity of the number of white pieces will not change after one operation: if the operation is not in this row and not in this column, then two pieces in the set have their colors flipped, the parity is unchanged; if the operation is on the intersection point, then 36 pieces in the set have their colors flipped, the parity is unchanged; if the operation is on other points, then 18 cells in the set have their colors flipped, the parity is unchanged. This deduces a contradiction. Therefore the largest integer n is 343.
